q: Identify the organelle in fraction 1, with two reasons.
Nuclei: they hold almost all the DNA (92%), and as the largest, densest organelles they settle at the lowest speed.
Enzyme X catalyses a step of the Krebs cycle. Identify the organelle in fraction 2.
Mitochondria: 88% of enzyme X is there, and they are medium-sized, settling at 10 000 g.
Enzyme Z is mainly in fraction 2, but some is in fractions 3 and 4. Suggest an explanation.
Z is a lysosome enzyme: lysosomes are about the size of mitochondria, and some burst during the breaking-up, releasing Z into the liquid.
Suggest a role for enzyme Y.
Fraction 3 holds membranes (ER, Golgi): Y could make lipids or modify proteins (adding sugars).
Explain why the cells are broken up in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution.
Cold slows enzymes that would digest the organelles; isotonic stops organelles bursting or shrinking by osmosis; the buffer keeps the pH steady so proteins are not denatured.

21.t: Working with data: lysosome enzymes and pH
q: State the optimum pH of each enzyme.
Lysosomal: pH 5. Cytoplasmic: pH 7.
Read the activity of the lysosomal enzyme at the pH of the cytoplasm.
About 8% at pH 7.
Explain why a leaking lysosome does little damage to the cell.
At the cytoplasm’s pH the enzyme keeps only about 8% of its activity, so it digests very little.
Explain why the lysosomal enzyme’s activity falls above pH 6.
Fewer H⁺ ions change the charges on R groups in the active site, altering its shape and its binding to the substrate.
Explain how the lysosome keeps its inside at pH 5.
Proton pumps in its membrane use ATP to actively transport H⁺ ions into the lysosome.
Explain how these data show an advantage of compartments.
Each compartment keeps its own conditions, so both enzymes can work at their optimum, and harmful digestive enzymes stay separated from the rest of the cell.
